items.sentence: A hand-held version combines an insulated grip, an internal resistance heater, and a slim metal tip that conducts heat to work.
Many tips use copper for rapid heat transfer, with iron plating that resists wear and corrosion from molten alloy.
Interchangeable tips come in pointed, chisel, and hoof profiles, providing different contact areas and access angles.
Temperature-controlled models place a sensor near the working end and use electronic circuitry to regulate heater power.
When connected to power, its heater raises the metal tip to a temperature sufficient to melt joining alloy.
During a joint, the hot tip heats both metal surfaces while feed wire melts and spreads across their contact.
Wiping the working end on a damp sponge or brass wool removes residue and helps preserve heat transfer.
After use, placing the hot tool in a stable stand keeps its tip away from the bench and nearby materials.
Repair technicians use one at an electronics bench when replacing damaged connectors or repairing broken circuit-board traces.
Battery-powered models are useful for field repairs at locations where mains electricity is unavailable.
Work is usually done on a heat-resistant surface with ventilation because heated flux can produce irritating fumes.
When assembling small boards, operators often choose a fine tip and restrained heat to limit damage to neighboring parts.
It creates a conductive metal bridge between component leads and circuit-board pads, completing an electrical path.
Heating wire ends with it allows molten alloy to coat strands before they are joined to terminals.
It can attach through-hole component leads to plated board holes by melting alloy around each lead.
In repair work, localized heating lets a technician free a single joint without warming an entire assembly.
